title: The Pre-Flight Ritual & Arming Safety
html:
Why a ritual beats a vibe

The single biggest predictor of who keeps all ten fingers is not skill — it is whether they run the same check, the same way, every single flight. Spinning 5-inch props on a 6S quad reach roughly 30,000+ RPM and will open a finger to the bone faster than you can react. A ritual converts safety from a decision you make under excitement into a reflex you don't have to think about.

The pre-flight check (memorize the order)

  1. Battery (pre). Confirm the pack is charged to full (4.20V/cell, or your storage-charged pack topped up). No puffing, no nicks in the wrapper, balance leads intact.
  2. Visual airframe. Arms tight, motors free of grass/hair wrapped on the bell, antennas (VTX + RX) not chopped or pinched, no cracked props. Spin each prop by hand — listen for bearing grind.
  3. Prop check. Correct rotation direction, no nicks, screws torqued. A chipped prop at 30k RPM becomes an unbalanced bomb.
  4. Strap the battery firmly with a fresh, grippy strap. A pack that ejects mid-flight = instant fall.
  5. Goggles/RC on FIRST, quad LAST. Always power the transmitter and goggles before plugging the quad in, so the model binds to a live link, never the reverse.
  6. Link + failsafe. Confirm RX is bound (solid LED), VTX channel matches goggles, and you get clean video.
  7. Mode switches. Verify ARM switch is OFF, flight mode is correct (Acro/Angle), and any BEEPER/TURTLE switches are where you expect.
  8. Area + people. Eyes up: bystanders, pets, cars, the spotter acknowledged. Announce "props hot!" before arming.

Verifying failsafe (do this for real, not on faith)

With props removed, arm the quad on the bench, then power off your radio. The motors must stop within ~1 second (Betaflight default failsafe stage 2 = DROP). If they keep spinning, your failsafe is misconfigured — fix it before you ever fly. Check it in Failsafe tab: Stage 2 set to Drop for freestyle, or GPS Rescue only if a reliable GPS lock is present.

Props off for all bench testing.
Any time you arm indoors, on a bench, or to test config — props come OFF. "Just this once" with props on is how people end up in the ER. The motor can spool to full throttle from a config glitch.

The arm/disarm sequence

Standard habit: throttle all the way down, then flip arm. To disarm, throttle down first, then flip arm off. Train yourself to disarm the instant the quad is on the ground — do not let props idle while you walk over. Enable Runaway Takeoff Prevention and a MOTOR_STOP-off configuration with prop-wash idle so the quad doesn't tip-over-spin.

betaflight arming flags
# type 'status' in CLI to see why it won't arm status Arming disable flags: RXLOSS THROTTLE ANGLE # RXLOSS = no radio link THROTTLE = stick not at zero ANGLE = too tilted Arming disable flags: (clear = ready to arm)
Read the flags.
If your quad refuses to arm, it is almost always telling you why. The OSD shows the arming-prevention reason on screen; status in CLI lists every flag. Don't "jiggle and retry" — read the reason.
▸Hands-On

Build your personal pre-flight checklist and burn the arm sequence into muscle memory.

  1. Write your own 8-item checklist on a card or phone note, in the order above.
  2. With props OFF (or in a sim), rehearse: radio on, goggles on, quad on, arm, disarm — 5 times.
  3. Test failsafe for real: arm props-off, kill radio, confirm motors stop in ~1s.
  4. Practice saying "props hot" out loud each arm so it becomes automatic outdoors.

title: Line-of-Sight Basics: Hover, Orientation & Nose-In
html:
Why line-of-sight first

Before goggles, before acro, you build the foundational reflex every pilot relies on: keeping track of which way the quad is facing. In a stable/angle mode hover you learn that roll and pitch sticks command lean, throttle commands climb/descend, and yaw rotates the nose. LOS practice forces you to mentally rotate the controls based on the quad's heading — a skill that pays off when you lose video or fly behind an object.

Stick discipline for a clean hover

On Mode 2 (the global standard): left stick = throttle (up/down) + yaw (left/right); right stick = pitch (forward/back) + roll (left/right). A good hover is mostly throttle management with tiny corrective pulses on roll/pitch. Beginners over-correct — they shove the stick, the quad lurches, they shove the opposite way, and it oscillates. The fix: small inputs, then wait. The quad responds with a slight lag; give it time before adding more.

Orientation: the four headings

HeadingRoll right stick →What happens
Tail toward you (nose away)Goes rightControls feel "normal"
Nose toward you (nose-in)Goes left (your view)Roll/pitch reversed
Left side toward youMoves away/towardPitch and roll swap roles
Right side toward youMoves toward/awayPitch and roll swap, opposite

The nose-in problem

Nose-in is where new pilots crash. When the quad faces you, pushing roll right sends it to your left, and pitch forward brings it toward you. The trick that works: steer the bottom of the quad / steer toward the high side. If the quad drifts left from your view, give the stick input that pushes it back — practice slowly until your brain stops translating and just reacts. Many pilots whisper "reversed" as a cue when the nose comes around.

Lock altitude first.
Pick one job at a time. Nail a rock-steady throttle hover at one height before you add any yaw. Trying to manage altitude AND orientation at once is what makes hovers wander into the dirt.

Self-leveling vs the goal

Angle (self-level) mode is a great training wheel for LOS hover — release the sticks and the quad levels itself. But it has a tilt limit and won't flip. You'll graduate to Acro later, but mastering orientation in Angle first means you're not fighting two new skills simultaneously.

Real LOS hover safety.
If you take this to a real quad, fly in a large open field, props checked, spotter present, and keep the quad at least 5-10m away and above head height — a quad drifting at face level is dangerous. Disarm immediately if it gets behind you or you lose orientation.

Drills that build the reflex

  • Box hover: hold position over a single spot for 60s, correcting drift with tiny pulses.
  • Slow yaw circle: rotate the nose 360° slowly while staying over one spot — this forces you through all four orientations.
  • Nose-in hold: rotate to nose-in and hold for as long as you can without drifting more than a meter.
▸Hands-On

Build orientation reflex in the sim (Liftoff, Velocidrone, or DRL).

  1. Hold a stationary hover over one spot for a full 60 seconds in Angle mode.
  2. Slowly yaw the nose 360° while staying over the spot.
  3. Rotate to nose-in (nose pointing at camera) and hold; log how many seconds before you drift more than a meter.
  4. Repeat the nose-in hold daily and watch the number climb.

title: The FPV Acro Progression: Hover to Forward Flight
html:
What Acro mode actually is

In Acro (rate) mode there is no self-leveling. The sticks command rotational rate, not angle: if you tilt the quad 20° forward and center the stick, it stays at 20°. This is the only mode for real FPV flying because it lets you point the thrust vector anywhere — but it means you are now the leveling system. Every input you make, you must also undo.

The acro hover

An acro hover is harder than an angle hover and is the gateway drill. The quad constantly wants to tip; you make tiny correcting taps to keep it level. Goal: hover in place in acro for 30s without drifting more than a couple meters. If you can acro-hover, forward flight is just leaning that hover.

Forward flight = lean + power

To move forward you do two things together:

  1. Pitch forward a small amount (5-15°). This tilts the thrust vector so part of it pushes you horizontally.
  2. Add throttle to compensate — when tilted, less thrust opposes gravity, so the quad sinks unless you give more power. This throttle-pitch coordination is the heart of FPV flight.

The classic beginner error: pitch forward, forget throttle, watch the quad mush into the ground. Or: pitch forward and never level back out, accelerating into a wall. Forward flight is a controlled, held lean — not a shove.

Stopping on a mark

To stop, you pitch back (the opposite of how you accelerated) to brake, while easing throttle, then return to a level hover. A clean stop on a target requires you to anticipate — start braking before the mark, because momentum carries you. Pilots judge this by how the ground/target grows in the FPV view.

PhasePitch stickThrottle
HoverCentered~Hover point
Accelerate forwardForward (held)Add to hold altitude
CruiseSlight forwardSteady
Brake to stopBack (held briefly)Ease off, then back to hover
Set sane rates first.
For learning, dial in moderate rates — roughly 670 deg/s max with low-to-mid RC Expo (~0.20) and Super Rate around 0.70 in Betaflight. Twitchy max rates make a beginner's corrections turn into oscillation. Smooth out before you speed up.
Throttle is your altitude, always.
In acro, the moment you tilt the quad in ANY direction, you need more throttle to hold height. Train your left thumb to pump throttle slightly with every lean. This becomes subconscious — but only with reps.

Common faults and fixes

  • Quad sinks when moving: not adding throttle on the lean. Add power proportional to tilt.
  • Overshooting the mark: braking too late. Begin the pitch-back earlier.
  • Wobble at the stop: slamming pitch back then centering hard. Smooth the brake and feather back to neutral.
▸Hands-On

Drill precise forward flight and stops in the sim.

  1. Hold an acro hover for 30s without drifting more than ~2m.
  2. Set a target ~50m away. Take off, fly forward, and stop precisely on the target.
  3. Do it three times; log how close you stopped each run (e.g. +3m, +1m, on target).
  4. Note whether you sank during acceleration — if so, focus the next session on throttle-with-lean.

title: Turns, Banking & Controlled Dives
html:
Coordinated turns: roll + yaw + throttle

A flat (rudder-only) turn looks robotic and bleeds speed. A coordinated banked turn — the FPV staple — combines three inputs at once:

  • Roll to bank the quad into the turn (this points the thrust vector toward the turn center).
  • Yaw to rotate the nose around so it tracks the new direction.
  • Throttle increased, because banking tilts thrust away from vertical and the quad would otherwise descend.

The mental model: you're not steering like a car, you're leaning a motorcycle. Bank in, add a touch of yaw to pull the nose around, hold throttle to keep the arc level. The more you bank, the more yaw and throttle you feed in.

The figure-eight: the universal coordination drill

A figure-eight forces you to roll left then right, transition through level, and coordinate yaw both directions. The center crossing is the hard part — you must smoothly reverse the bank without ballooning up or dropping. Fly it big and slow first, then tighten the loops as you smooth out.

Look where you're going.
In the goggles, point your attention at the exit of the turn, not the quad's nose. Your hands follow your eyes. Pilots who stare at the obstacle they're trying to avoid tend to fly straight into it (target fixation).

Controlled dives

A dive is how you trade altitude for speed and set up shots and tricks. The key insight: throttle is NOT your descent control in a dive — pitch is. You pitch forward/down to point the quad at the ground, and you reduce throttle so you don't accelerate into the dirt. The dangerous part is the pull-out.

The dive-to-level pullout

  1. Commit: pitch nose down to your dive angle, throttle low.
  2. Manage speed: the steeper and longer the dive, the faster you arrive — judge by how fast the ground fills your view.
  3. Pull out EARLY: begin pitching back to level while adding throttle. The throttle punch arrests your descent. Beginners pull out late and "pancake" into the ground.
Altitude is your friend.
Practice dives with lots of vertical buffer. A misjudged pullout at 5m ends in a crash; the same error at 50m gives you room to recover. In a sim this is free reps — abuse that.
ManeuverPrimary inputDon't forget
Banked turnRollAdd throttle + a touch of yaw
Figure-eightRoll reversalStay level through the center
DivePitch downCut throttle going in, punch it pulling out
Throttle-blip on the pullout.
The signature of a clean dive recovery is a sharp throttle punch exactly as you level the nose. Time it too early and you balloon; too late and you hit ground. Practice the timing isolated: dive, then "level-and-punch" as one combined motion.

Smoothness over speed

Every input in this lesson must be fed in and out gradually at first. Smooth roll into a turn, smooth roll out. Jerky inputs cause prop-wash wobble and ugly footage. Speed is earned only after the motions are clean.

▸Hands-On

Coordinate turns and dives in the sim.

  1. Fly five smooth figure-eights, keeping altitude constant through the center crossing.
  2. Set up a high hover, then dive to the ground and pull out to level flight without touching down.
  3. Repeat the dive 5 times; rate (1-5) how smoothly you held altitude after each pullout.
  4. Log which side of your figure-eight is weaker and drill that direction extra.

title: Your First Real Flights & In-Air Troubleshooting
html:
The sim-to-air gap

If you've put in sim hours, your reflexes will transfer — but the real world adds wind, real consequences, and the adrenaline of seeing your actual quad in the air. Expect to fly more conservatively your first session. That's correct. The goal of a maiden is not freestyle; it's confirming the quad flies straight and you can land it.

Site and conditions

  • Large open field, no people, no roads, no power lines, soft ground (grass).
  • Wind under ~10 mph for a first flight. Wind makes a hover wander and punishes weak throttle control.
  • Spotter present — someone watching LOS who can warn you of people approaching or the quad heading somewhere bad.
  • Know your local rules: in the US, recreational flyers should pass TRUST, register the aircraft if over 250g, and follow the FAA's recreational guidelines (B4UFLY for airspace). Verify current FAA and local regulations before flying — rules change.
Airspace is real.
Don't fly in controlled airspace without authorization (LAANC), stay clear of airports, and keep visual line of sight. Check B4UFLY or your country's equivalent the day you fly. This lesson is general guidance, not legal advice — confirm the current rules yourself.

The maiden sequence

  1. Run your full pre-flight ritual from Lesson 5.1. Verify failsafe.
  2. Set the quad ~3m in front of you, nose away.
  3. Arm. Spool up gently and lift just off the ground (a few cm) to check it doesn't pull hard in any direction — a hop test reveals reversed motors, bad tune, or a flipped prop before you commit to altitude.
  4. Climb to ~3-5m and hold a hover. Make small corrections. Get comfortable.
  5. Fly gentle forward passes and easy turns. Keep it in front of you.
  6. Land with throttle low and steady; disarm the instant the skids touch.

In-air troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeResponse
Quad drifts one direction at hoverWind, or trim/accelerometer offsetCorrect with stick; re-level accel on the ground later
Fast oscillation / hot motorsPID tune too high (P/D)Land, lower gains; don't keep flying hot motors
Slow wallowing wobbleP too low or prop washLand, retune; avoid descending through your own wash
Video static/breakupRange, antenna, or interferenceTurn back toward yourself, gain altitude, land if it worsens
Quad won't respond / flies offRX link lossDon't chase — failsafe should drop it; note where it lands
Disarm on doubt.
If the quad does something you don't understand — flies the wrong way, oscillates, or you lose orientation — and it's safe to drop it (over grass, away from people), disarm. A dropped quad over an empty field is a $0 problem. A confused quad heading toward a person is a hospital problem. When unsure, kill it.
Hot motor check.
After your first pack, touch each motor (carefully). Warm is fine; too-hot-to-hold means a tune or prop issue — fix it before the next flight. Heat is your quad telling you something's wrong.

Log the flight

Start a flight log from day one: date, location, pack used, mAh consumed, landing voltage, any issues, and one thing to improve. This log turns scattered sessions into a measurable progression and helps you spot battery/quad problems early.

▸Hands-On

Fly a safe maiden session and start your flight log.

  1. Pick a legal, open site with light wind and a spotter; run your pre-flight ritual.
  2. Hop-test, then hover, then fly gentle passes. Land and disarm on touchdown.
  3. Log: date, site, pack, mAh used, landing voltage, and any issue you hit.
  4. Write one sentence on how you responded to any in-air problem (drift, wobble, video) and what you'll do differently next time.

title: Freestyle Tricks: Rolls, Flips & Power Loops
html:
The mindset: commit fully

The number-one cause of a botched roll or flip is not committing — pilots tap the stick, panic when the world goes upside down, and let go. In acro, a roll is just a held rotation; if you give a full deflection and keep it there, the quad completes the rotation and you simply stop the stick when level returns. Hesitation is what kills it.

The roll (easiest first trick)

  1. Build a little forward speed and get some altitude (10m+).
  2. Full roll-stick left or right and hold.
  3. The quad rotates 360° on its roll axis. As the horizon comes back level, center the stick sharply.
  4. Punch throttle as you exit — you lose altitude during the rotation because thrust isn't pointing down while inverted.

The flip

Same as a roll but on the pitch axis — full back (backflip) or full forward (frontflip). Backflips are more natural for beginners because you can see the ground come back over the top. Same rules: commit, hold, center on level, punch throttle on exit.

The power loop

The power loop is the signature freestyle move — a vertical loop, usually over or through an obstacle. It's a throttle-and-pitch trick, not just a flip:

  1. Approach with speed at low-to-mid altitude.
  2. Pull full back pitch AND add throttle to climb up and over the top of the loop.
  3. At the top you're inverted, looking back — ease throttle as you come over so you don't shoot off.
  4. Coming down the back side, the ground rushes up — throttle back in and level out at the bottom (this is a dive pullout, Lesson 5.4).

The power loop combines everything: commitment (the flip), throttle management (top and bottom), and a dive pullout. That's why it's the rite-of-passage trick.

TrickAxis / inputsThe gotcha
RollFull roll, hold, center on levelLetting go halfway = inverted crash
FlipFull pitch (back/fwd), holdForgetting the exit throttle punch
Power loopPitch + throttle through a vertical circleToo much throttle over the top; late pullout at bottom
Practice high, fail safe.
Do every new trick with 20-30m of altitude. Height is recovery room. Once you can land the trick consistently up high, then bring it down toward obstacles. In a sim, altitude is free — bank hundreds of reps before you risk a real quad.
Isolate the exit.
Most failed tricks die on the exit, not the rotation. Drill just the recovery: roll/flip, then immediately get level + punch throttle + hover. When the exit is automatic, the trick is reliable.
Real-quad tricks.
Never attempt rolls, flips, or power loops near people or yourself. A trick gone wrong sends a spinning quad in an unpredictable direction. Open field, spotter, altitude, and only after you've got it solid in the sim.

Building a combo

Once individual tricks land cleanly, chain them: roll out of a dive, flip over a tree, power loop a gap. Freestyle flow is just clean tricks connected by smooth transitions — and clean tricks come from committed, well-practiced singles.

▸Hands-On

Drill the three core tricks to a reliable success rate in the sim.

  1. Practice rolls until you can complete and land level 5 times in a row.
  2. Same for flips (try backflips first).
  3. Power loop: pick a tree or gate and loop it; commit to the throttle over the top.
  4. Log your success rate (e.g. "rolls 9/10, loops 4/10") and re-test next session.

title: Smooth Cinematic Movements & Racing Lines
html:
Two opposite disciplines, same sticks

Cinematic flying is about silky, deliberate, minimal-input movement that looks like a camera on a crane. Racing is about maximum efficiency — the shortest, fastest line through gates. They train opposite instincts (smooth vs aggressive) but both demand precision. Practicing both makes you a complete pilot.

Cinematic fundamentals

  • Reduce your rates. Cinematic pilots often fly a dedicated low-rate profile (e.g. max ~200-300 deg/s) so big stick moves become gentle. Many add RC Smoothing and fly with a slightly heavier/cinewhoop setup for inertia.
  • Move on one axis at a time where possible — a clean orbit, a clean push-in, a clean reveal. Mixing axes is fine once smooth, but jerky multi-axis moves read as amateur.
  • Constant velocity, not constant stick. Ease into a move and ease out — no abrupt starts or stops. Think of accelerating a heavy dolly.

The cinematic orbit

To circle a subject: hold a steady roll toward the subject, a matching steady yaw to keep the nose pointed at it, and constant throttle for level altitude. The art is balancing roll and yaw so the radius stays constant and the subject stays centered in frame. Practice big and slow.

Smooth is a setting AND a skill.
You can buy smoothness with low rates and RC smoothing, but the real polish comes from your thumbs learning to feather inputs. Record your sim flights and watch them back — jitter you can't feel while flying is obvious on playback.

Racing lines

Racing is geometry. The fastest path is rarely the one that hits the visual center of each gate — it's the line that minimizes direction changes and keeps your energy up.

  • Late apex the gate like a racing car corners: enter wide, clip the inside of the gate, exit aimed at the next gate. This straightens the path between gates.
  • Look ahead two gates. Your line through the current gate should set up the next. Pilots who only look at the gate in front of them scrub speed on every exit.
  • Carry energy. Don't fully stop and re-accelerate. Use dives to build speed on straights and bank turns to maintain momentum around pylons.
  • Throttle management: punch out of corners, feather before tight gates. Smooth throttle = faster laps than on/off flying.
GoalCinematicRacing
RatesLow, smoothedHigh, responsive
InputsFeathered, one axisDecisive, combined
ThrottleConstant, gentlePunch + feather
EyesOn framingTwo gates ahead
Run the same course repeatedly.
Racing improvement comes from repetition on a fixed track. Fly the same gate course 10 laps, note where you lose time (usually a specific corner), and drill that section in isolation. Time every lap — what gets measured gets faster.
Speed near obstacles.
Racing lines hug gates and pylons. On a real course, fly within your proven skill margin — clipping a gate at speed sends shards and a heavy quad in unpredictable directions. Build speed in the sim before any real race.
▸Hands-On

Practice both disciplines in the sim and measure results.

  1. Fly a slow cinematic orbit around a subject; keep it centered and the radius constant. Rate your smoothness 1-5.
  2. Load a gate course and fly 5 timed laps, late-apexing each gate.
  3. Log your best lap time and identify the one corner costing you the most.
  4. Drill that corner 10 times, then re-run the course and compare your time.

title: Reading Your OSD & Crash Avoidance in the Air
html:
Your OSD is your instrument panel

The On-Screen Display overlays telemetry on your FPV feed. The skill is glance-reading — flicking your eyes to a number for a fraction of a second without losing flight focus, the way a driver checks a speedometer. The two numbers that keep you out of trouble: battery voltage and flight timer.

The vital OSD elements

ElementWhat it tells youWhy it matters
Battery voltagePack charge stateLand before it sags too low — #1 crash-prevention number
Flight timerTime armedBackup for voltage; learn your pack's typical flight time
RSSI / Link qualityRadio signal strengthFalling RSSI = you're approaching failsafe range
mAh consumedCapacity usedMost reliable "fuel gauge" if you have a current sensor
WarningsArming flags, low-batt, RX lossFlash on screen — never ignore them

Reading voltage under load

Voltage sags under throttle and recovers when you ease off, so read it at a steady cruise, not mid-punch. The meaningful number is the resting/cruise voltage. Rule of thumb per cell:

  • 4.20V = full
  • 3.80V = storage / comfortable
  • 3.50V (loaded) / ~3.7V resting = start heading home
  • 3.30V loaded = LAND NOW; below this you risk damaging the pack and a brownout
Land on warnings — every time.
When the OSD flashes LOW BATTERY or your set per-cell threshold trips, land. Don't squeeze in one more trick. A pack pushed below ~3.3V/cell loaded can sag into a brownout — the FC loses power mid-air and the quad falls out of the sky. Chronically over-discharging also puffs and kills LiPos.

Set your warnings before you fly

betaflight OSD / battery warnings
# Configurator > Power & Battery minimum cell voltage 3.30 V # triggers warning warning cell voltage 3.50 V # early heads-up maximum cell voltage 4.35 V # OSD tab: enable Battery Voltage, mAh drawn, Timer, RSSI, Warnings

Crash avoidance: signal cues

Video and link degrade before total loss, giving you warning:

  • Video gets sparkly/staticky: you're at the edge of analog VTX range or behind an obstruction. Turn back toward yourself and gain altitude — line of sight to the receiver matters.
  • RSSI / link quality dropping fast: on digital (DJI/HDZero) you'll see warnings or a frozen frame. Stop pushing range; fly home immediately.
  • Don't fly into a void: behind metal buildings, into deep "signal shadows," or straight away at max range. Lose the link and failsafe drops the quad wherever it is.
Call it out loud.
Saying your voltage and timer aloud while flying ("3.7, two minutes") forces the glance-read habit and keeps the numbers in your awareness. Many top pilots narrate their packs. It feels silly and it works.
Learn YOUR pack.
Every quad/pack combo has a personality. After a few flights you'll know "this pack gives me 3:30 to 3.5V." That internalized feel — backed by the OSD — is what lets you fly confidently right up to a safe landing.
▸Hands-On

Build the glance-read habit and a hard voltage discipline.

  1. In the sim or on a real quad, set a per-cell land threshold (e.g. 3.5V resting).
  2. Fly a session calling your voltage and timer aloud every 30 seconds.
  3. The moment you hit your threshold or see a low-batt warning, land immediately — no exceptions.
  4. Log the landing voltage and flight time so you learn your pack's real endurance.
